newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt shines amid the jobs data gloom.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt shines amid the jobs data gloom.

text.p: *Australian debt yields struck lower after the June employment data stoked up hopes of a further easing in monetary policy, although some profit-taking was seen towards the close.
*Treasurer Costello comments takes heat out of rally.
Australian debt yields struck lower after the June employment data stoked up hopes of a further easing in monetary policy, although some profit-taking was seen towards the close.

The benchmark October 2007 bond dropped through 6.60 percent at one stage, its lowest level in some 3-1/2 years, after June total employment rose just 11,900 against an expected rebound of over 40,000, while full-time employment dropped once again.
September and December bill futures briefly hit contract highs of 94.99 and 95.00 as a 1/2 point rate cut was priced in.

"The cut in cash rates could come as early as tomorrow, but we think it more likely following the CPI and average weekly earning data due July 23 and 24," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank.

While the government took to heart a fall in the unemployment rate to 8.5 percent, this was largely seen due to a "discouraged worker effect" with the participation rate dropping to 63.0 percent, or, as James put it, "because people gave up looking for jobs."
Treasurer Peter Costello said he thought the fall in unemployment was a very good sign.
Costello also said that the most recent policy easing on May 23 had not impacted on the economy yet.
"Before anyone gets fixed on the next movement, let's just sit bank and wait for the previous movements to have the positive effect which they will have," he added.

His comments took some heat out of the post-data rally, although even at its close the September bill contract at 94.95 was equating a cash rate of just 5.05 percent compared to an official rate of 5.50 percent.
The weak jobs outcome and a benign inflation outlook has led some analysts to believe the next cut will not be the last.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the sub-par growth and good inflation prospects has been the basis for arguing a 50 basis point rate cut after the August RBA board meeting.

"Today's data has reinforced this view and raised in our minds the prospect that the RBA may feel a larger cut is warranted -- 75 or 100 basis points -- and/or the next easing might not be the last in the current cycle," said Deutsche's economist Tony Meer.
The rally saw bond yield spreads to the U.S. narrow sharply with the 10-year margin below 35 basis points at one stage, and raising ideas that parity is not far down the track.

The local market also outperformed Canada, which had rallied with U.S. Treasuries on Wednesday, but lost ground to the long-end of the New Zealand curve after a well received NZ$150 million tender of a new line of July 2009 stock.
